source_text: Ὥστε τοὺς πλουσίους μαθηματικῶς ἀκουστέον, τοὺς δυσκόλως εἰσελευσομένους εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν, μὴ σκαιῶς μηδὲ ἀγροίκως μηδὲ σαρκίνως· οὐ γὰρ οὕτως λέλεκται. οὐδὲ ἐπὶ τοῖς ἐκτὸς ἡ σωτηρία. οὔτε εἰ πολλὰ οὔτε εἰ ὀλίγα ταῦτα ἢ μικρὰ ἢ μεγάλα ἢ ἔνδοξα ἢ ἄδοξα ἢ εὐδόκιμα ἢ ἀδόκιμα, ἀλλ᾿ ἐπὶ τῇ τῆς ψυχῆς ἀρετῇ. πίστει καὶ ἐλπίδι καὶ ἀγάπῃ καὶ φιλαδελφίᾳ καὶ γνώσει καὶ πραότητι καὶ ἀτυφίᾳ καὶ ἀληθείᾳ, ὧν ἆθλον ἡ σωτηρία. οὐδὲ γὰρ διὰ κάλλος σώματος ζήσεταί τις ἢ τοὐναντίον ἀπολεῖται· ἀλλ᾿ ὁ μὲν τῷ δοθέντι σώματι ἁγνῶς καὶ κατὰ θεὸν χρώμενος ζήσεται. ὁ δὲ φθείρων τὸν ναὸν θεοῦ φθαρήσεται. δύναται δέ τις καὶ αἰσχρὸς ἀσελγαίνειν καὶ κατὰ κάλλος σωφρονεῖν· οὐδὲ ἰσχὺς καὶ μέγεθος σώματος ζωοποιεῖ οὐδὲ τῶν μελῶν οὐδενία ἀπολλύει. ἀλλ᾿ ἡ τούτοις ψυχὴ χρωμένη τὴν αἰτίαν ἐφ᾿ ἑκάτερα παρέχεται. ὑπόφερε γοῦν. φησί. παιόμενος τὸ πρόσωπον. ὅπερ δύναται καὶ ἰσχυρός τις ὢν καὶ εὐεκτῶν ὑπακοῦσαι καὶ πάλιν ἀσθενικός τις ὢν ἀκρασίᾳ γνώμης παραβῆναι. οὕτως καὶ ἄπορός τις ὢν καὶ ἄβιος εὑρεθείη ποτ᾿ ἂν μεθύων ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις. καὶ χρήμασι πλούσιος νήφων καὶ πτωχεύων ἡδονῶν. πεπεισμένος. συνετός, καθαρός, κεκολασμένος. εἰ τοίνυν ἐστὶ τὸ ζησόμενον μάλιστα καὶ πρῶτον ἡ ψυχὴ καὶ περὶ ταύτην ἀρετὴ μὲν φυομένη σῴζει, κακία δὲ θανατοῖ, δῆλον ἤδη σαφῶς ὅτι αὕτη καὶ πτωχεύουσα ὧν ἄν τις ὑπὸ πλούτου διαφθείρηται σῴζεται, καὶ πλουτοῦσα τούτων ὧν ἐπιτρίβει πλοῦτος θανατοῦται· καὶ μηκέτι ζητῶμεν ἀλλαχοῦ τὴν αἰτίαν τοῦ τέλους πλὴν ἐν τῇ τῆς ψυχῆς καταστάσει καὶ διαθέσει πρός τε ὑπακοὴν θεοῦ καὶ καθαρότητα πρός τε παράβασιν· ἐντολῶν καὶ κακίας συλλογήν.
thought_title: Salvation depends on the soul's virtue, not on external things
orientation: Clement is explaining that the rich who enter the kingdom with difficulty are to be understood spiritually, because salvation depends on the soul's disposition, not on outward circumstances.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore the rich persons must be heard mathematically, the ones who will enter into the kingdom with difficulty, not in a left-handed way nor in a boorish way nor in a fleshly way; for it has not been said thus. Nor does salvation depend on external things. Neither if these things are many nor if they are few or small or great or glorious or inglorious or esteemed or unesteemed, but on the virtue of the soul. On faith and hope and love and brotherly love and knowledge and gentleness and freedom from ignorance and truth, of which the prize is salvation. For neither because of beauty of body will someone live or on the contrary will perish; but the one who uses the body given to him purely and according to God will live. But the one who destroys the temple of God will be destroyed. And someone ugly can act licentiously and someone beautiful can be self-controlled; neither strength and size of body gives life nor does weakness of any of the members destroy. But the soul using these things provides the cause on either side. Endure then, he says, being struck on the face. Which a strong and vigorous person is able to obey and again a weak person is able to transgress by weakness of judgment. Thus also someone who is without resources and without livelihood would be found at some time drunk with desires. And someone rich in money sober and poor in pleasures, persuaded, intelligent, pure, disciplined. If therefore the thing that will live especially and first is the soul and concerning this virtue when it grows saves, but vice kills, it is clear already plainly that this soul both being poor in the things by which someone would be corrupted by wealth is saved, and being rich in the things which wealth wears away is killed; and let us no longer seek elsewhere the cause of the end except in the state and disposition of the soul toward obedience to God and purity and toward transgression of commandments and collection of vice.

lemmas.gloss: mathematically, in a learned or precise way
without livelihood, without means of life

choices.why: Clement uses the adverb to mean 'in a precise, learned, or scientific way,' contrasting with crude or fleshly interpretation; the literal rendering preserves his unusual word choice.
The Greek word literally means 'left-handedly' and carries the sense of awkward or wrong; keeping the literal image preserves Clement's contrast with the right understanding.
The glossary bans 'detachment' for ἀπάθεια, and ἀτυφία is a distinct virtue; 'freedom from pride' renders the alpha-privative noun literally and clearly.
The word means the prize or reward of a contest; Clement uses it to describe salvation as the reward of the virtues listed.
The imperative is quoted from Jesus' teaching on turning the other cheek; the literal imperative preserves the command force.
The word means lacking the means of life; rendering it literally distinguishes it from πτωχός (poor person) and from being merely without money.

pass_b_english: So then, the rich persons who will enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty must be understood with exact discernment—not clumsily, not boorishly, not fleshly. For that is not how the saying was spoken. Nor does salvation depend on external things: not on whether they are many or few, small or great, honored or dishonored, esteemed or unesteemed. It depends on the virtue of the soul—on faith, hope, love, brotherly love, knowledge, gentleness, freedom from ignorance, and truth, whose prize is salvation. For no one will live because of bodily beauty, nor will anyone perish for the opposite reason. Rather, the one who uses the body he has been given purely and according to God will live, but the one who destroys the temple of God will be destroyed. A person who is ugly can act licentiously, and a person who is beautiful can be self-controlled. Neither bodily strength nor size gives life, nor does the lack of any bodily member destroy. It is the soul that uses these things that provides the cause in either direction. "Endure," he says, "when you are struck on the face." A person who is strong and vigorous can obey this, and again a person who is weak can transgress it through lack of self-control in judgment. So also a person who is without resources and without livelihood may be found drunk on desires, while a person rich in money may be sober, poor in pleasures, persuaded, intelligent, pure, and disciplined. If, then, the soul is what will live above all and first, and virtue growing in it saves while wickedness kills, it is now clearly evident that the soul which is poor in the things by which a person is corrupted through wealth is saved, and the soul which is rich in the things that wealth wears down is put to death. And let us no longer seek the cause of the end anywhere else except in the soul's condition and disposition toward obedience to God and purity, and toward transgression of the commandments and the collection of wickedness.

problems.why: ἀτύφία means freedom from ignorance, not freedom from pride
problems.ruling: ἀτυφία means freedom from pride/haughtiness, not ignorance; claim confuses with ἀμαθία, but English is correct.

fixed: Changed 'freedom from pride' to 'freedom from ignorance' because ἀτυφία means freedom from ignorance (τῦφος = delusion, ignorance), not pride.

edits.old: must be understood mathematically—not in a left-handed way
edits.new: must be understood with exact discernment—not clumsily

fixed: The source μαθηματικῶς means 'with exact discernment' or 'precisely,' not 'mathematically,' and σκαιῶς means 'clumsily' or 'awkwardly,' not 'in a left-handed way.' The English misstates the source, so I corrected it.
